subject: Career
title: Signal vs. Noise in Messages
description: A micro-lesson that makes Signal vs. Noise in Messages usable.

hook.text: A 500-word email where the actual request is buried in paragraph four. Your signal is drowning in noise.

buildup.text: Shannon's information theory applies: every message has signal (useful info) and noise (everything else).

discovery.text: High-signal communication means every word earns its place. No filler, no preamble, no hedging.

twist.text: People add noise for comfort: disclaimers, softeners, backstory. But the reader just wants the point.

climax.text: Write your message. Then cut it in half. The remaining words are probably all that was needed.

punchline.text: Say less. Mean more. Get heard.

quiz.question: What is 'noise' in workplace communication?
options: Unnecessary filler that buries the actual message

details.summary: Signal-to-noise ratio in workplace communication measures how much of a message contains useful information versus filler, repetition, or irrelevant content. High-signal communicators are perceived as more competent and their messages receive faster, more accurate responses.
details.whyItMatters: Information overload is the default in modern workplaces. Professionals who maximize signal and minimize noise earn more attention, trust, and influence per message.
takeaways: Cut filler phrases like 'just wanted to check in' from messages
Lead with the conclusion or request, then provide context
One clear message outperforms three vague follow-ups every time

faq.question: How do I improve the signal-to-noise ratio in my emails?
faq.answer: Before sending, delete every sentence that does not add new information or move the recipient toward action. Remove hedging language and redundant context. If the email still makes sense after cuts, the removed sentences were noise.

faq.question: Is it rude to send very short, direct messages to colleagues?
faq.answer: Brevity is not rudeness; it is respect for the reader's time. Adding a brief warm opener like 'Hope you're well' and a 'Thanks' at the end provides social lubrication without adding significant noise. Context determines how much warmth to include.
